Chapter 5 answers the question Arjuna opens it with: whether renunciation of action or the yoga of action is better. Kṛṣṇa ranks karma-yoga slightly ahead, but only to collapse the apparent opposition — sāṃkhya and yoga, rightly practiced, yield the same fruit, and true renunciation turns out to be an inward freedom from hatred and desire, not outward abstention from acts, indeed one that is hard to reach without yoga first. The chapter's central figure is the disciplined yogin who acts with body, mind and senses yet remains untouched, like a lotus-leaf on water, because he has surrendered his actions and their fruit; a run of verses lists the ordinary bodily and sense-functions such a person still performs while holding that it is the senses, not the self, that move among their objects. From there the chapter turns to the metaphysics behind this freedom: the self neither creates agency nor claims sin or merit, and ignorance alone is what veils knowledge, which knowledge then dispels like sunlight. The wise, seeing the one brahman equally in a learned brahmin and an outcaste, in a cow and a dog, become steady amid pleasure and pain and find a happiness that owes nothing to outer contact. Three closing verses describe the yogin who has turned wholly inward as attaining brahma-nirvāṇa — extinction, or liberation, in brahman — available already in this life to whoever has cut away doubt, desire and anger. The chapter closes with a description of the breath-controlled ascetic and a final image of Kṛṣṇa himself as the enjoyer of all sacrifice, the great lord of all worlds, and the friend of every being, knowing whom is the way to peace.
